title: Sensō-ji and the backstreets of Asakusa
description: Walk through the great red gates towards Sensō-ji, then step away from Nakamise's souvenir stalls into the older streets around the temple. Pair the temple with a Sumida riverside walk or a small soba lunch to see more than its busiest approach.
whyGo: An immediately recognisable introduction to Tokyo's temple traditions and older commercial neighbourhoods.
tradeoff: The central approach is intensely busy; an early start changes the experience substantially.
novemberNote: Comfortable walking weather is likely, with a cooler riverside after sunset; temple events and the Culture Day holiday can add crowds.
bookingNote: Ordinary temple exploration does not usually require advance booking; check access details and any special events nearer the visit.
sourceLabel: Sensō-ji official visitor information

title: Meiji Jingū, Harajuku and Omotesandō
description: Enter Meiji Jingū through its broad forest approaches, then walk out into Harajuku's exuberant shops and Omotesandō's architecture. The side streets around Cat Street offer a gentler route between independent shops and cafés.
whyGo: A single walk links a major Shinto shrine, contemporary street culture and design-led Tokyo.
tradeoff: These are contrasting experiences spread across a sizeable area; selecting a few stops works better than trying every shopping street.
novemberNote: November can bring families celebrating Shichi-Go-San at the shrine; seasonal foliage timing varies across the area.
bookingNote: General shrine and neighbourhood visits are normally walk-in; check shrine opening times because access follows daylight.
sourceLabel: Meiji Jingū official website

title: Shibuya Crossing and the city from above
description: Experience Shibuya's famous crossing at street level, then take in the scale of Tokyo from Shibuya Sky. Keep time afterwards for the smaller streets around the station, where the city's energy continues beyond the postcard view.
whyGo: One of the clearest ways to appreciate Tokyo's enormous scale, especially as the city lights come on.
tradeoff: Popular sunset tickets can be competitive, and weather can restrict the outdoor rooftop.
novemberNote: Sunset comes early, so a late-afternoon visit needs deliberate scheduling; distant Fuji views depend on visibility and are never guaranteed.
bookingNote: Book a timed official ticket once the release window is confirmed; review rooftop weather and baggage rules before visiting.
sourceLabel: Shibuya Sky official ticket and visitor information

title: Tsukiji breakfast, with a sushi-making option
description: Explore Tsukiji’s outer market for a seafood breakfast, tamagoyaki and specialist shops selling knives, tea and cooking ingredients. For a more participatory day, pair the market with a separately researched sushi-making class where you prepare and eat your own lunch.
whyGo: A strong fit for two keen food travellers: learn the ingredients, then consider turning that curiosity into a hands-on meal.
tradeoff: It is heavily visited and some snacks carry tourist-area prices; this is the outer market, while the wholesale fish market operates in Toyosu.
novemberNote: A morning visit uses the shorter day well; individual shops have different closure days and holiday schedules.
bookingNote: Market browsing is generally walk-in; a cooking class needs a separately vetted provider, confirmed meeting point and advance booking. The map pin marks the market only, not a chosen class.
sourceLabel: Tsukiji Outer Market official website; cooking provider still to research

title: teamLab Borderless at Azabudai Hills
description: Wander through a digital art environment where light, colour and projected forms move between rooms. Its open-ended layout rewards curiosity and makes an easy pairing with nearby architecture, gardens or dinner.
whyGo: A distinctive contemporary counterpoint to temples and traditional streets, with an immersive experience to share.
tradeoff: Dark rooms, moving projections and crowds will not suit everyone; it is a popular attraction rather than a quiet gallery.
novemberNote: A useful indoor option for a wet or cold day, although a fixed ticket reduces weather flexibility.
bookingNote: Reserve timed entry through the official site after checking current availability, access and exhibition guidance.
sourceLabel: teamLab Borderless official exhibition page

title: Japan's art and history in Ueno
description: Use Tokyo National Museum's collections to put Buddhist sculpture, ceramics, painting and samurai objects into context. Follow a focused museum visit with Ueno Park or the lively shopping streets around Ameyoko.
whyGo: Provides background that makes later shrine, temple and craft visits more meaningful.
tradeoff: The collections are large and displays rotate; two or three chosen themes make a better visit than trying to see everything.
novemberNote: Offers a strong indoor fallback; the park's autumn colour depends on tree species and the year's weather.
bookingNote: Confirm the museum calendar, including Monday closures and holiday exceptions; special exhibitions can require separate tickets.
sourceLabel: Tokyo National Museum official website

title: A Shinjuku evening of tiny bars and neon
description: Begin with the lantern-lit lanes of Omoide Yokochō, then explore Shinjuku's illuminated streets and, if it suits you, a small Golden Gai bar. These are intimate places with very few seats, so choosing one welcoming venue is enough for a memorable evening.
whyGo: Captures the theatrical night-time city alongside a much smaller scale of eating and drinking.
tradeoff: Some venues allow smoking, charge cover fees or prefer regulars; menus and atmosphere matter more than ticking off famous alleyways.
novemberNote: An atmospheric option after an early sunset; outdoor lanes can feel chilly between venues.
bookingNote: Many small venues are walk-in; check displayed cover charges and house rules, and book a larger dinner separately if needed.
sourceLabel: GO TOKYO official tourism guide; Shinjuku details to verify

title: Fushimi Inari beyond the first torii gates
description: Follow the vermilion torii uphill from Fushimi Inari's main shrine into a network of wooded paths and smaller shrines. Walking beyond the most photographed tunnels reveals a more spacious, contemplative place.
whyGo: An iconic Kyoto experience that can also become a rewarding forest walk.
tradeoff: The lower paths are crowded and the full mountain circuit involves many steps; there is no need to complete the summit route to enjoy it.
novemberNote: Plan the wooded walk in daylight and bring a layer; the shrine is not primarily a peak-foliage destination.
bookingNote: Ordinary shrine access does not normally require booking; verify any special access restrictions before travelling.
sourceLabel: Fushimi Inari Taisha official website

title: Kiyomizu-dera and the lanes of Higashiyama
description: Visit Kiyomizu-dera's great wooden terrace above the city, then descend through the sloping streets of Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka. Break the walk with a small tea stop or ceramics shop instead of rushing from one camera spot to the next.
whyGo: Combines one of Kyoto's essential temples with its most recognisable traditional streetscape.
tradeoff: Narrow lanes become very busy, and the hills and steps can make a supposedly short visit tiring.
novemberNote: Colour may still be developing during the first half of November; any autumn evening opening must be checked against the 2026 calendar.
bookingNote: Check official admission arrangements and any announced evening sessions; ordinary sightseeing usually does not need a guide reservation.
sourceLabel: Kiyomizu-dera official website

title: Gion, a tea-making option and a riverside evening
duration: 2–3 hours; 3–4 with a booked tea session
description: Begin with a small-group or private tea session that includes learning to whisk your own matcha, then walk Gion’s public streets and the Shirakawa canal. Cross the Kamo River towards a reserved dinner near Pontochō, letting architecture, water and food set the pace.
whyGo: A gentle but immersive shared evening that joins participation in tea culture with one of Kyoto’s most atmospheric neighbourhoods.
tradeoff: Tea experiences differ substantially in depth and group size, while Gion is a working district with street-specific access and photography restrictions; choose both provider and route carefully.
novemberNote: Early darkness creates atmosphere, while riverside sitting becomes colder than daytime sightseeing suggests.
bookingNote: Select and reserve a tea provider whose session includes participation, and book any priority restaurant. The map pin marks the Shirakawa area, not a chosen tea venue; confirm public walking routes and posted photography rules locally.
sourceLabel: Kyoto City official tourism guide; tea provider and Gion visitor guidance to verify

title: Arashiyama's garden, bamboo and river
description: Anchor an Arashiyama visit around Tenryū-ji's pond garden, then connect the bamboo grove with a walk towards the river. Starting early leaves room to enjoy the scenery before the busiest lanes fill.
whyGo: Brings together Kyoto's garden tradition, mountain backdrop and one of Japan's best-known bamboo walks.
tradeoff: The famous grove is a short, busy section; the garden and wider river landscape justify the journey more than the grove alone.
novemberNote: Autumn colour may be emerging but peak timing varies; avoid assuming the hills will be fully red during these dates.
bookingNote: Check garden access and any temporary closures; scenic railway or boat additions have separate booking and operating requirements.
sourceLabel: Tenryū-ji official website; wider Arashiyama details to verify

title: Kinkaku-ji's Golden Pavilion
description: Follow the garden circuit around the Golden Pavilion and its pond, where reflections make the building's setting as striking as its gold exterior. Pair it with a nearby northwest Kyoto stop so that the cross-city journey earns its place.
whyGo: A remarkable and immediately recognisable example of Kyoto's designed temple landscapes.
tradeoff: The visitor route is largely a procession around exterior viewpoints, and it takes a separate journey from eastern Kyoto.
novemberNote: Autumn demand can be high even before peak leaf colour; allow for busy local transport.
bookingNote: Confirm current entry arrangements and access; an ordinary visit generally does not require an advance time slot.
sourceLabel: Kinkaku-ji official website

title: Nishiki Market and a Kyoto cooking option
description: Browse Nishiki’s covered market for pickles, tofu products, tea and the ingredients that distinguish Kyoto cooking. Pair it with a separately booked class in Japanese home cooking or Kyoto-style obanzai to turn unfamiliar ingredients into dishes you can make together.
whyGo: Combines regional food discovery with a practical, shared experience that carries home beyond the trip.
tradeoff: It gets congested and increasingly caters to visitors; buy selectively and eat in each shop's designated area.
novemberNote: The covered arcade is useful in rain, but it is not an evening food market and individual opening days vary.
bookingNote: The market is normally walk-in; verify a cooking provider’s menu, language, actual hands-on participation and class location before booking. The map pin marks the market and does not imply a class runs inside it.
sourceLabel: Nishiki Market official website; cooking provider still to research

title: Nanzen-ji and the eastern temple paths
description: Explore Nanzen-ji's grand temple setting, brick aqueduct and selected gardens before continuing north towards the Philosopher's Path. Choosing one or two interiors leaves time for the lane-side cafés and small details between temples.
whyGo: An attractive way to experience eastern Kyoto at walking pace, with architecture, gardens and quieter stretches between major sights.
tradeoff: The full north–south route is longer than it looks on a map, and garden or temple admissions can accumulate.
novemberNote: This is a celebrated autumn area, but colour and illumination schedules need checking; popular neighbouring Eikan-dō can draw large crowds.
bookingNote: Verify opening arrangements for the specific gardens and temples selected; seasonal evening admissions may operate separately.
sourceLabel: Nanzen-ji official website; wider walking route to verify

title: Dōtonbori and an Osaka food night
description: See Dōtonbori's giant signs and canal reflections, then make dinner the main event with okonomiyaki, takoyaki or another Osaka favourite. Step into the lanes around Hōzen-ji for a smaller-scale contrast to the main strip.
whyGo: A joyful, easy introduction to Osaka's reputation for eating well and enjoying a night out.
tradeoff: The busiest frontage is tourist-heavy; a researched restaurant matters more than simply joining the longest queue.
novemberNote: An easy evening option after a day trip, with a warm seated meal welcome on cooler nights.
bookingNote: Reserve a specific dinner if it is a priority; casual stalls and many smaller venues operate queues instead.
sourceLabel: Osaka official tourism guide; Dōtonbori venues to verify

title: Osaka Castle and its great stone walls
description: Walk through the castle park to appreciate the broad moats and immense stonework before deciding whether to enter the reconstructed main tower's museum. The landscape gives a better sense of the former fortress's scale than a quick tower photograph alone.
whyGo: Connects Osaka's modern cityscape with the political struggles that shaped early modern Japan.
tradeoff: The main tower is a modern reconstruction with museum interiors; travellers seeking an original surviving castle may prefer a different excursion.
novemberNote: Park trees can provide seasonal colour, with conditions varying across the month; exposed paths feel cooler on windy days.
bookingNote: Check museum entry arrangements and any restoration or exhibition notices before choosing an interior visit.
sourceLabel: Osaka Castle Museum official website

title: Shinsekai's retro streets and kushikatsu
description: Explore the colourful streets beneath Tsūtenkaku and stop for Osaka-style fried skewers. A walk through Janjan Yokochō adds older shopfronts and a different mood from polished shopping districts.
whyGo: Offers a vivid, retro side of Osaka and another regional food experience with relatively little planning.
tradeoff: Some stretches are tourist-oriented and the appeal is atmosphere more than major monuments; it may overlap with Dōtonbori if time is short.
novemberNote: Works for a late lunch or early evening; choose indoor dining if the weather turns cold or wet.
bookingNote: A neighbourhood walk is flexible; check ticket requirements separately if adding the tower or its attractions.
sourceLabel: Osaka official tourism guide; Shinsekai details to verify

title: Tōdai-ji's Great Buddha and Nara Park
description: Walk through Nara Park to Tōdai-ji's monumental gate and Great Buddha Hall, where the scale of the bronze Buddha is the real centrepiece. Continue to Nigatsu-dō for a hillside perspective and a calmer stretch of the temple precinct.
whyGo: One of Japan's most impressive historic religious sites, with a rewarding landscape around it.
tradeoff: Station-to-temple walking adds up, and the deer are free-ranging animals rather than a petting attraction; keep food and belongings controlled.
novemberNote: A comfortable day-trip season, with early dusk limiting how many outer sites fit; foliage timing remains variable.
bookingNote: Ordinary temple visits generally work without reservations; confirm hall opening times and any special exhibition tickets.
sourceLabel: Tōdai-ji official website

title: Kasuga Taisha's lantern-lined forest approach
description: Follow stone lanterns into the woodland around Kasuga Taisha, where vermilion shrine buildings and hanging bronze lanterns change the mood of a Nara day. Take time on the approach rather than treating it as a quick extra after Tōdai-ji.
whyGo: Adds forest atmosphere and Shinto heritage to a day otherwise dominated by the Great Buddha.
tradeoff: It lengthens the Nara walking circuit, and some inner areas require separate admission or have restricted access.
novemberNote: Forest paths darken earlier than open parkland; public lantern illumination events should not be assumed for these travel dates.
bookingNote: Confirm current shrine access and any special openings; routine exploration usually needs no advance reservation.
sourceLabel: Kasuga Taisha official website

title: A Hakone ryokan night with hot springs
description: Slow the trip down with a traditional inn, a leisurely dinner and time in Hakone's hot-spring baths. A room with a private bath or a reservable private bathing session can make this especially comfortable as a couple.
whyGo: A deliberate one-night splurge for shared food, hospitality and bathing, especially welcome between active city and walking days.
tradeoff: A meal-inclusive stay or private-bath room may exceed the £100–150 nightly room target and needs a live quote; dinner times are fixed, and shared baths are commonly separated by gender.
novemberNote: Cool air suits hot-spring bathing, while autumn demand can tighten availability; allow time to arrive well before dinner.
bookingNote: Book a specific property after checking meal inclusions, dietary accommodation, private-bath availability, tattoo policy and cancellation terms. The map pin is Hakone-Yumoto as an area anchor, not a selected hotel.
sourceLabel: Hakone official tourism website; individual ryokan to research

title: Lake Ashi and Hakone's volcanic landscape
description: Combine a Lake Ashi crossing with Hakone's mountain transport and the volcanic scenery around Ōwakudani. Build the day around the landscape and changing viewpoints, with a clear-weather Fuji sighting treated as a bonus.
whyGo: An accessible introduction to Japan's volcanic geography with a memorable mix of trains, cable transport and lake travel.
tradeoff: Multiple connections and queues can fill the day; weather, wind or volcanic conditions can disrupt sections, so the full circuit needs flexibility.
novemberNote: Mountain foliage can be further advanced than in Tokyo or Kyoto, but the air is colder and daylight short; visibility still varies.
bookingNote: Check operating notices, route connections and pass value shortly before travel; allow a flexible alternative if ropeways or boats are suspended. The map pin marks Lake Ashi near Tōgendai, not the whole circuit.
sourceLabel: Hakone Navi official transport and sightseeing information

title: Sculpture in the hills at Hakone Open-Air Museum
description: Walk among large-scale sculptures set against Hakone's green slopes, with indoor galleries providing changes of pace. The combination of landscape and art makes a relaxed alternative to spending the whole day changing transport.
whyGo: A strong option for art-minded travellers and a satisfying half-day complement to a ryokan stay.
tradeoff: Much of the experience is outdoors, so heavy rain limits its appeal even though indoor spaces exist.
novemberNote: Layers help on cool mountain paths; seasonal colour can enhance the setting without being the visit's sole purpose.
bookingNote: Check current exhibitions, gallery closures and ticket arrangements through the museum before fixing the day.
sourceLabel: Hakone Open-Air Museum official website
